attempts.reason_tested: already published: canine babesiosis severity data exist
attempts.method: grep for ferritin in /core/articles/CB*.md (hits CB132, CB242, CB286) and /core/data/markdown/CB*.md (hits CB039, CB107, CB132, CB147, CB242, CB286); read each context; also checked the grid's other cb_confirmed IDs CB454 and the iron article CB073. PubMed query (dog OR dogs OR canine) AND (babesia OR babesiosis) AND (ferritin OR hyperferritinemia OR haemophagocytic OR hemophagocytic), 2026-11-12.
attempts.result: No canine babesiosis study measures serum ferritin against severity or outcome. CB242 (10.36483/vanvetj.1292352) measured ferritin in 7 infected vs 7 control dogs, no significant difference, species not identified, no severity split. CB132 (10.1016/j.tcam.2025.101025) is a single B. vulpes case with haemophagocytic syndrome in which hyperferritinaemia was one diagnostic feature: a case description, not a contrast. CB286 mentions ferritin only in discussing iron-status tests and measured none. CB039 uses ferritin as a molecular-weight marker on a gel. CB147 uses Perls stain for tissue iron (ferritin and haemosiderin in Kupffer cells) in B. rossi livers, which is histology, not circulating ferritin, and is not analysed by outcome. CB073 reports lower serum IRON (not ferritin) in dogs with SIRS. PubMed added only the CB132 case and a 2002 splenectomy case with haemophagocytic activity (PMID 12012956, no DOI).

attempts.reason_tested: the published canine null already answers the question
attempts.method: Read the CB242 note and text for design, group sizes and detectable effect.
attempts.result: No. CB242 is an infected-versus-healthy comparison with 7 dogs per group, one of about 30 analytes tested without a stated correction, and with no species identification. It has no severity or outcome contrast at all, so it cannot be a null for this candidate, and at 7 vs 7 it would only detect a very large difference. The gap stands.

attempts.reason_tested: human severity evidence weak or unverified
attempts.method: Resolved the grid's lead DOI 10.1186/s12879-026-13418-z and the malaria meta-analysis 10.1017/S0007114522000757 in PubMed; the paediatric DOIs 10.1097/INF.0000000000004916 and 10.24911/SJP.106-1776661764 returned no PubMed record and are unverified here. Searched for further sepsis cohorts: 10.3389/fnut.2026.1858343, 10.1159/000552315.
attempts.result: Sepsis evidence is strong and replicated: MIMIC-IV, 718 septic patients, median ferritin 818 vs 476 ng/mL in non-survivors vs survivors, OR 1.97 above 526 ng/mL (10.1186/s12879-026-13418-z); a second MIMIC-IV cohort of 3360 patients, hyperferritinaemia HR 1.56 for 30-day mortality (10.3389/fnut.2026.1858343); and 437 patients in which ferritin above 4420 ng/mL marked a macrophage-activation-like phenotype with 75% versus 43% ICU mortality (10.1159/000552315). The malaria evidence is weaker and is not a severity contrast: the meta-analysis shows ferritin raised in clinical versus asymptomatic infection (mean difference 366 ug/L in children with clinical malaria) and concludes that iron markers must be adjusted for infection and inflammation (10.1017/S0007114522000757). Grade 3 holds on sepsis, not on malaria severity.

attempts.reason_tested: confounded or near-circular in babesiosis (haemolysis and acute-phase response)
attempts.method: Reasoning from the human meta-analysis above, the SV-06b DS07 result (/experiments/SV-06/report.md b.4-b.6) and the B. rossi complicated definition.
attempts.result: A real limit, not a rejection. Ferritin is both an acute-phase protein and an iron-storage protein, so in babesiosis it will rise with inflammation and with iron released by haemolysis; the human meta-analysis makes exactly this point for malaria (10.1017/S0007114522000757). The complicated label in DS07 includes haematocrit and bilirubin, and SV-06b found haemoglobin beta the strongest DS07 signal, so a ferritin difference could restate haemolysis rather than add a mechanism. A canine study must adjust for haematocrit, bilirubin, CRP and a sample haemolysis index, and the interpretable question is haemophagocytic hyperinflammation (the CB132 hypothesis), not ferritin alone.

attempts.method: Resolved assay DOIs in PubMed: 10.1016/j.rvsc.2016.09.003, 10.1016/j.rvsc.2025.105993; 10.3390/biom16070997 was not resolved.
attempts.result: Canine-specific ferritin immunoassays are in routine research use: ferritin with CRP in canine leishmaniosis treatment monitoring (10.1016/j.rvsc.2016.09.003) and ferritin with hepcidin and iron in a canine fracture-healing series (10.1016/j.rvsc.2025.105993); ferritin also rose with stage in canine leishmaniosis in 10.1002/vms3.70871, and CB242 itself measured it on an autoanalyser. No formal canine method-validation paper was found in this pass, so the assay is 'used in dogs' rather than demonstrably validated, and ferritin is species-specific, so assay choice matters.

attempts.method: grep GN=FTL and GN=FTH1 in /core/data/raw/DS07/B_Proteins.txt; grep of /experiments/shared/tidy/*.json.
attempts.result: Neither ferritin chain is in DS07 and neither appears in a tidy feature file; serum ferritin is in any case a secreted, mostly iron-poor L-chain form that shotgun serum proteomics does not capture well. DS06 holds FTL and FTH1 RNA in 5 experimental Beagles with no severity contrast, and ferritin translation is controlled by iron-responsive elements, so RNA is a poor proxy. Stored serum only; it is cheap to add to an existing panel.

verdict_reason: Ferritin has never been measured against severity or outcome in canine babesiosis: the only measurement (CB242, 7 vs 7, infected versus healthy, no difference) has no severity contrast and no power, and CB132 is a single severe case with hyperferritinaemia. The human sepsis evidence is strong across three cohorts, and canine ferritin assays are in use. The lead is weakened because the malaria evidence is an infection contrast rather than a severity one, because no formal canine assay validation was found, and because ferritin in a haemolytic disease is heavily confounded by haemolysis and the acute-phase response.

human_counterpart.claim: Sepsis, 718 patients: ferritin 818 vs 476 ng/mL in non-survivors vs survivors, OR 1.97 above 526 ng/mL for 28-day mortality
Sepsis, 3360 ICU patients: hyperferritinaemia HR 1.56 for 30-day mortality, transferrin and TIBC protective
Septic shock, 437 patients: ferritin above 4420 ng/mL marks a macrophage-activation-like phenotype, ICU mortality 75% vs 43%
Malaria meta-analysis: ferritin much higher in clinical than asymptomatic infection, and confounded by inflammation; not a severity contrast

canine_parallel_already_made: partly: CB242 measured ferritin in infected versus healthy dogs only (no difference, 7 vs 7) and CB132 reports hyperferritinaemia in one severe B. vulpes case with haemophagocytic syndrome; no CB article relates ferritin to severity or outcome
